analysis.one_liner: Bans phthalate plastics chemicals from anything that touches food.
analysis.headline: The bill was never acted on after being introduced and referred to the Senate HELP Committee; the 115th Congress ended without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Phthalates are plastic-softening chemicals used in food packaging and food-processing materials. Studies link them to hormone disruption, particularly in pregnant women, infants, and children. This bill would declare all ortho-phthalates unsafe in any material that touches food, strike prior FDA approvals allowing their use, and require the FDA to weigh effects on vulnerable populations when evaluating substitutes. It was referred to the Senate Health Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers — especially pregnant women, infants, and children — would be exposed to less phthalate through food packaging and processing. Food workers who handle packaged products and production materials would also see lower exposure. Food and packaging manufacturers would face the cost of switching to alternatives.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, especially children and pregnant women

how_it_helps.text: Declares all ortho-phthalate chemicals unsafe as food contact substances two years after enactment, making them prohibited in food packaging and processing materials [S3].
Wipes out existing FDA regulations that had approved specific phthalate uses in food contact materials, and bars the FDA from approving any new phthalate uses [S3].
Requires the FDA to consider exposure risks to vulnerable populations — pregnant women, infants, children, the elderly, and highly exposed workers — when reviewing substitutes for phthalates [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Food packaging manufacturers and food producers would bear the cost of reformulating packaging and processing equipment to replace phthalates with alternatives within two years.

drawbacks.text: The ban is categorical: it removes FDA's existing case-by-case safety approvals for phthalates and bars future approvals regardless of dose or specific use, so chemicals with limited, low-dose uses would be treated the same as the riskiest ones [S3].

The two-year compliance window would require packaging and food-processing suppliers to quickly identify and validate substitute materials, a real cost that could be passed to consumers in food prices.

Restricting phthalates in packaging pushes manufacturers toward substitute plasticizers whose own long-term health effects were, at the time, less studied — which is why the bill directs FDA to scrutinize alternatives [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health rationale is straightforward: phthalates leach into food from packaging and processing materials, and the bill targets the most sensitive groups. The cost is a mandatory reformulation across the food packaging supply chain within two years, and a blanket ban rather than dose-based limits trades precision for certainty. On balance it is a precautionary consumer-protection measure whose main burden falls on manufacturers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2018 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it sat until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019 without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on June 28, 2018, joined by Sen. Richard Blumenthal [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action was taken — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food packaging manufacturers and food companies that use phthalates kept the status quo — no requirement to reformulate packaging or processing materials, and no compliance costs.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks in the Senate record.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no opposition is recorded; the bill had two Democratic sponsors and simply stalled in committee [S4][S5].

industries.note: The ban would force packaging makers to reformulate away from phthalate plasticizers within two years. Their cost of compliance is the price of reducing chemical exposure for consumers.

Processors use phthalate-containing materials in tubing, gaskets, and conveyors that touch food, and would need to replace equipment. Their preference for continuing current practices runs against the public's interest in lower exposure.

Companies selling phthalate-free packaging and substitute plasticizers would gain a guaranteed market as the industry complies. The bill requires FDA to vet those substitutes for safety to vulnerable groups.
